lines.text: In fact, the need for recognition of one's value is something
implanted in the very nature of man. We can only live and
breathe freely in a circle where we are appreciated. We only
feel ourselves to be uninhibited and secure when we have the
feeling that we are esteemed at our full value. And just as we
need that others should respect and appreciate us in our
peculiar and characteristic worth, so we in our turn must
respect the special merits of others and give them full
recognition. But the decisive thing in this matter is that the
recognition which we all need can never be made the real
aim of our action and conduct. It can accrue to us only as the
by-product of our behaviour, of our straightforward positive
contribution, of our actual attitude towards our fellow men.
Appreciation cannot be a goal to be striven after and at-
tained with exertion and effort; it can only be given us as a gift.
The mistake made by so many is that they aim at appre-
ciation as an end in itself, and they are anxious to attain it
as a desirable good to the attainment of which they must
concentrate their efforts. This urge for recognition can afflict
a human life like a disease. It leads us astray into an impurity
of motives, with the consequence that we do our work not
disinterestedly for its own sake, but for our sake, and in
order to gain credit for ourselves. A man who acts to increase
his own prestige may well do great things; and it is just
what we usually term record achievements which are often
traceable merely to the urge for recognition. The greatness
and true value of a work does not after all consist in the fact
that it goes one better than other works of its kind, that it
shows the intensity of the exertion and the extremity of the
cost at which it has been achieved, but is decided simply by
whether it is sensible and useful in its place, and serves the
general good of the community.
If the mind of a man is obsessed by this urge for recogni-
tion, so that all his accomplishments, as it were, declare:
"Look, that is what I can do!" then his whole life becomes
corrupted by something hollow and unreal. He does not
work with his eye on the thing itself but with a sidelong
glance on others in whose presence he desires to distinguish
